security_audit.summary: Most static findings are Markdown code fences, documentation links, or expected GitHub CLI examples and were marked false positive. The webhook handler example is a real issue because it uses child_process.execSync with unvalidated GitHub webhook and PR comment data. No prompt injection text was found in SKILL.md.

remediation.issue: Webhook handler executes request-derived command text with execSync.
remediation.suggestion: Replace execSync template strings with spawn or execFile using fixed argument arrays, strict command allowlists, and numeric PR validation.

remediation.issue: Webhook example does not verify GitHub webhook signatures before acting on events.
remediation.suggestion: Verify X-Hub-Signature-256 with a shared secret before parsing or executing any webhook action.

remediation.issue: Production workflow examples rely on external CLI execution.
remediation.suggestion: Pin ruv-swarm versions, use a lockfile or trusted installed binary, and document required package integrity controls.

remediation.issue: GitHub token permissions are not explicitly restricted in workflow examples.
remediation.suggestion: Add a permissions block with the minimum pull request and contents scopes needed for review comments and labels.

static_findings.snippet: run: echo "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" | gh auth login --with-token

finding_verdicts.reason: The webhook example imports child_process and later runs execSync from request-derived data. This is dangerous in a network-facing handler because it enables shell execution paths.

The handler runs execSync with a value taken from webhook JSON without validation. The value is likely numeric in normal GitHub events, but the pattern is still unsafe in an unauthenticated sample handler.
The handler inserts the raw PR comment body into an execSync shell command. A crafted comment can escape the quoted argument and execute arbitrary shell commands.

semantic_findings.title: Untrusted PR Comment Command Execution
semantic_findings.description: The webhook handler accepts comments starting with /swarm and passes the full comment body into execSync. A crafted PR comment could break the quoted argument and run shell commands on the webhook host if this sample is deployed.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The command variable comes from event.comment.body and is interpolated into a shell command on line 407. The code shows no allowlist, escaping, or argument array use.

semantic_findings.title: Missing Webhook Signature Verification
semantic_findings.description: The webhook handler parses request data and executes actions for /github-webhook without verifying a GitHub webhook signature. An attacker could send forged requests to trigger automation if the handler is exposed.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The handler branches on req.url and event fields, then executes commands, but the shown code has no signature or shared-secret verification before acting.

content.user_title: Review GitHub Pull Requests with AI Swarms
content.value_statement: Pull request reviews can miss security, performance, and architecture issues when context is spread across files. This skill coordinates focused AI agents and GitHub CLI workflows to produce structured review feedback.
actual_capabilities: Guides GitHub pull request review setup with GitHub CLI commands.
Defines specialized review agents for security, performance, style, architecture, and accessibility.
Shows workflows for posting PR comments, labels, review status, and quality gates.
Provides examples for GitHub Actions based automated review pipelines.
Includes troubleshooting steps for swarm status, authentication, rate limits, and long reviews.
limitations: Requires GitHub CLI, ruv-swarm, and claude-flow to be installed and authenticated.
Examples can modify pull requests, labels, reviews, and merge settings when run.
Review quality depends on repository context, agent configuration, and reviewer oversight.
Webhook examples need security hardening before production use.

use_cases.title: Triage Complex Pull Requests
use_cases.description: Coordinate focused review agents for large changes that need security, performance, and architecture coverage.

use_cases.title: Add Security Review Gates
use_cases.description: Run security-focused review flows and request changes when critical findings appear.

use_cases.title: Automate Review Feedback in CI
use_cases.description: Use GitHub Actions examples to collect PR context, run review agents, and post summarized feedback.

prompt_templates.title: Review One Pull Request
prompt_templates.prompt: Review pull request 123 with security, performance, style, and architecture focus. Summarize blockers, warnings, and suggested follow-up tasks.

prompt_templates.title: Run a Security-Focused Review
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze pull request 123 for authentication, authorization, secrets, dependency risk, and unsafe input handling. Request changes for critical issues.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare CI Review Automation
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a GitHub Actions review workflow for this repository. Include required agents, token permissions, labels, and quality gate behavior.

prompt_templates.title: Coordinate a High-Risk Release Review
prompt_templates.prompt: Review the release pull request with security, performance, architecture, tests, and accessibility agents. Produce merge criteria and owner follow-ups.

output_examples.input: Review a pull request that changes login and session handling.
output: Security review found one blocker in session invalidation.
Architecture review recommends separating token validation from request middleware.
Suggested merge gate: request changes until the session fix and tests are added.

output_examples.input: Summarize review progress for a large refactor.
output: Three agents completed review and one performance check is still running.
Current concerns are test coverage gaps and an unresolved database query regression.
Next action: post a progress comment and assign the database owner.

output_examples.input: Create quality gates for a repository review process.
output: Block merges on critical security findings.
Warn on performance regressions above the configured threshold.
Require manual reviewer approval before automated merge is enabled.

best_practices: Use least-privilege GitHub tokens and define repository permissions explicitly.
Review generated comments before posting them to active pull requests.
Validate webhook payloads and command inputs before enabling automation.
anti_patterns: Do not execute PR comment text directly as a shell command.
Do not allow automated approval or merge without human review gates.
Do not run unpinned external CLIs in production workflows without dependency controls.

faq.question: What tools does this skill require?
faq.answer: It expects GitHub CLI, ruv-swarm, and claude-flow to be available and authenticated.

faq.question: Can it post comments to pull requests?
faq.answer: Yes. The examples show how to post status comments, review summaries, labels, and inline comments with GitHub CLI.

faq.question: Does it replace human code review?
faq.answer: No. It helps organize automated analysis, but maintainers should review findings and approve merges manually.

faq.question: Is it useful for security reviews?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes a security agent workflow for OWASP issues, secrets, permissions, and critical finding gates.

faq.question: Can it run in GitHub Actions?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill includes workflow examples for automated review on pull request events.

faq.question: What should be hardened before production use?
faq.answer: Webhook handlers need signature verification, command allowlists, strict input validation, and rate limits.
